Main.sentence: Jefferson F. Davis (June 3, 1808 – December 6, 1889) was an American politician who served as the only ___E:president of the Confederate States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Confederate_States_of_America)___ from 1861 to 1865. He represented ___E:Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi)___ in the ___E:United States Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate)___ and the ___E:House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ as a member of the ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ before the ___E:American Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ .
He was the ___E:United States Secretary of War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_War)___ from 1853 to 1857.

Davis, the youngest of ten children, was born in ___E:Fairview, Kentucky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairview,_Kentucky)___ , but spent most of his childhood in ___E:Wilkinson County, Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilkinson_County,_Mississippi)___ .

His eldest brother ___E:Joseph Emory Davis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Emory_Davis)___ secured the younger Davis's appointment to the ___E:United States Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy)___ .
Upon graduating, he served six years as a lieutenant in the ___E:United States Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army)___ .

After leaving the army in 1835, Davis married ___E:Sarah Knox Taylor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Knox_Taylor)___ , daughter of future president ___E:Zachary Taylor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor)___ .
Sarah died from ___E:malaria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria)___ three months after the wedding.

Davis became a cotton ___E:planter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planter_class)___ , building ___E:Brierfield Plantation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brierfield_Plantation)___ in Mississippi on his brother Joseph's land and eventually owning as many as 113 slaves.
In 1845, Davis married ___E:Varina Howell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varina_Davis)___ .

During the same year, he was elected to the United States House of Representatives, serving for one year. From 1846 to 1847, he fought in the ___E:Mexican–American War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War)___ as the colonel of a volunteer regiment.
He was appointed to the United States Senate in 1847, resigning to unsuccessfully run as governor of Mississippi.
In 1853, President ___E:Franklin Pierce U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce)___ appointed him ___E:Secretary of War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_War)___ .
After Pierce's administration ended in 1857, Davis returned to the Senate.
He resigned in 1861 when Mississippi ___E:seceded U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession_in_the_United_States)___ from the United States.
During the Civil War, Davis guided the Confederacy's policies and served as its commander in chief.

When the Confederacy was defeated in 1865, Davis was captured, arrested for alleged complicity in the ___E:assassination of Abraham Lincoln U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln)___ , accused of ___E:treason U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treason#United_States)___ , and imprisoned at ___E:Fort Monroe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Monroe)___ .
He was released without trial after two years.

Immediately after the war, Davis was often blamed for the Confederacy's defeat, but after his release from prison, the ___E:Lost Cause of the Confederacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy)___ movement considered him to be a hero. In the late 19th and the 20th centuries, his legacy as Confederate leader was celebrated in the South.
In the twenty-first century, his leadership of the Confederacy has been seen as constituting treason, and he has been frequently criticized as a supporter of slavery and racism.

Many of ___E:the memorials dedicated to him U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_memorials_to_Jefferson_Davis)___ throughout the United States ___E:have been removed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Removal_of_Confederate_monuments_and_memorials)___ .
Jefferson F. [a] Davis was the youngest of ten children of Jane and Samuel Emory Davis.

Samuel Davis's father, Evan, who had a ___E:Welsh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales)___ background, came to the ___E:colony of Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Georgia)___ from Philadelphia.  [b] Samuel served in the ___E:Continental Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army)___ during the ___E:American Revolutionary War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War)___ , and received a land grant for his service near present-day ___E:Washington, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_Georgia)___ .

He married Jane Cook, a woman of ___E:Scotch-Irish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch-Irish_Americans)___ descent whom he had met in ___E:South Carolina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina)___ during his military service, in 1783.  Around 1793, Samuel and Jane moved to Kentucky.

Jefferson was born on June 3, 1808, [c] at the family homestead in Davisburg, a village Samuel had established that later became ___E:Fairview, Kentucky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairview,_Kentucky)___ .
He was named after then-President ___E:Thomas Jefferson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson)___ .
In 1810, the Davis family moved to ___E:Bayou Teche U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayou_Teche)___ , Louisiana.

Less than a year later, they moved to a farm near ___E:Woodville, Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodville,_Mississippi)___ , where Samuel cultivated cotton, acquired twelve slaves,  and built a house that Jane called ___E:Rosemont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosemont_(Woodville,_Mississippi))___ .
During the ___E:War of 1812 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812)___ , three of Davis's brothers served in the military.
When Davis was around five, he received a rudimentary education at a small schoolhouse near Woodville.

When he was about eight, his father sent him with Major ___E:Thomas Hinds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hinds)___ and his relatives to attend ___E:Saint Thomas College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Rose_Priory)___ , a Catholic preparatory school run by ___E:Dominicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Order)___ near ___E:Springfield, Kentucky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Kentucky)___ .

In 1818, Davis returned to Mississippi, where he briefly studied at ___E:Jefferson College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_College_(Mississippi))___ in ___E:Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_Mississippi)___ .
He then attended the Wilkinson County Academy near Woodville for five years.
In 1823, Davis attended ___E:Transylvania University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania_University)___ in ___E:Lexington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington,_Kentucky)___ .

While he was still in college in 1824, he learned that his father Samuel had died. Before his death, Samuel had fallen into debt and sold Rosemont and most of his slaves to his eldest son ___E:Joseph Emory Davis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Emory_Davis)___ , who already owned a large estate in ___E:Davis Bend, Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Bend,_Mississippi)___ , about 15 miles (24 km) south of ___E:Vicksburg, Mississippi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi)___ .
Joseph, who was 23 years older than Davis,  informally became his surrogate father.

His older brother Joseph got Davis appointed to the ___E:United States Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy)___ at West Point in 1824, where he became friends with classmates ___E:Albert Sidney Johnston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Sidney_Johnston)___ and ___E:Leonidas Polk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonidas_Polk)___ .
Davis frequently challenged the academy's discipline.
In his first year, he was court-martialed for drinking at the nearby tavern of ___E:Benny Havens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Havens)___ .
He was found guilty but was pardoned.
The following year, he was placed under house arrest for his role in the ___E:eggnog riot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggnog_riot)___ during Christmas 1826 but was not dismissed.
He graduated 23rd in a class of 33.
Second Lieutenant Davis was assigned to the ___E:1st Infantry Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States))___ .
He was accompanied by his personal servant James Pemberton, an enslaved ___E:African American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American)___ whom he inherited from his father.

In early 1829, he was stationed at Forts ___E:Crawford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Crawford)___ and ___E:Winnebago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Winnebago)___ in ___E:Michigan Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Territory)___ under the command of Colonel ___E:Zachary Taylor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor)___ ,  who later became ___E:president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ .
Throughout his life, Davis regularly suffered from ill health.
During the northern winters, he had ___E:pneumonia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia)___ , colds, and ___E:bronchitis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronchitis)___ .

He went to Mississippi on furlough in March 1832, missing the outbreak of the ___E:Black Hawk War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hawk_War)___ , and returned to duty just before the ___E:Battle of Bad Axe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bad_Axe)___ , which ended the war.  When ___E:Black Hawk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hawk_(Sauk_leader))___ was captured, Davis escorted him for detention in St. Louis.
Black Hawk stated that Davis treated him with kindness.
After Davis's return to Fort Crawford in January 1833, he and Taylor's daughter, Sarah, became romantically involved.
Davis asked Taylor if he could marry Sarah, but Taylor refused.

In spring, Taylor had him assigned to the ___E:United States Regiment of Dragoons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Cavalry_Regiment_(United_States)#Formation)___ under Colonel ___E:Henry Dodge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Dodge)___ .

He was promoted to first lieutenant and deployed at ___E:Fort Gibson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Gibson)___ in ___E:Arkansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_Territory)___ .
In February 1835, Davis was ___E:court-martialed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court-martial)___ for insubordination.
He was acquitted.
He requested a furlough, and immediately after it ended, he tendered his resignation, which was effective on June 30.
Davis decided to become a cotton ___E:planter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planter_class)___ .

He returned to Mississippi where his brother Joseph had developed Davis Bend into ___E:Hurricane Plantation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Plantation)___ , which eventually had 1,700 acres (690 ha) of cultivated fields with over 300 slaves.
Joseph loaned him funds to buy ten slaves and provided him with 800 acres (320 ha), though Joseph retained the title to the property.
Davis named his section ___E:Brierfield Plantation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brierfield_Plantation)___ .
Davis continued his correspondence with Sarah,  and they agreed to marry with Taylor giving his reluctant assent.

They married at ___E:Beechland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beechland_(Jeffersontown,_Kentucky))___ on June 17, 1835.  In August, he and Sarah traveled to ___E:Locust Grove Plantation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locust_Grove_State_Historic_Site)___ , his sister Anna Smith's home in ___E:West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Feliciana_Parish,_Louisiana)___ .
Within days, both became severely ill with ___E:malaria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria)___ .
Sarah died at the age of 21 on September 15, 1835, after only three months of marriage.
For several years after Sarah's death, Davis spent much of his time developing Brierfield.

In 1836, he possessed 23 slaves;  by 1840, he possessed 40;  and by 1860, 113.  He made his first slave, James Pemberton, Brierfield's effective overseer,  a position Pemberton held until his death around 1850.  Davis continued his intellectual development by reading about politics, law and economics at the large library Joseph and his wife, ___E:Eliza U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliza_Van_Benthuysen_Davis)___ , maintained at Hurricane Plantation.
Around this time, Davis became increasingly engaged in politics, benefiting from his brother's mentorship  and political influence.

Davis became publicly involved in politics in 1840 when he attended a ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ meeting in Vicksburg and served as a delegate to the party's state convention in ___E:Jackson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi)___ ; he served again in 1842.  One week before the state election in November 1843, he was chosen to be the Democratic candidate for the Mississippi House of Representatives for ___E:Warren County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_County,_Mississippi)___ when the original candidate withdrew his nomination, though Davis lost the election.
In early 1844, Davis was chosen to serve as a delegate to the state convention again.

On his way to Jackson, he met ___E:Varina Banks Howell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varina_Davis)___ , the 18-year-old daughter of William Burr Howell and ___E:Margaret Kempe Howell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Kempe_Howell)___ , when he delivered an invitation from Joseph for her to visit the Hurricane Plantation for the Christmas season.

At the convention, Davis was selected as one of Mississippi's six ___E:presidential electors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_electors)___ for the ___E:1844 presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1844_United_States_presidential_election)___ .
Within a month of their meeting, 35-year-old Davis and Varina became engaged despite her parents' initial concerns about his age and politics.
During the remainder of the year, Davis campaigned for the Democratic party, advocating for the nomination of ___E:John C. Calhoun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Calhoun)___ .

He preferred Calhoun because he championed Southern interests including the ___E:annexation of Texas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_annexation)___ , reduction of tariffs, and building naval defenses in southern ports.
When the party chose ___E:James K. Polk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk)___ for their presidential candidate, Davis campaigned for him.

Davis and Varina married on February 26, 1845.  They had six children: Samuel Emory, born in 1852, who died of an undiagnosed disease two years later;  Margaret Howell, born in 1855, who married, raised a family and lived to be 54;  Jefferson Davis Jr., born in 1857, who died of ___E:yellow fever U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever)___ at age 21;  Joseph Evan, born 1859, who died from an accidental fall at age five;  William Howell, born 1861, who died of ___E:diphtheria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria)___ at age 10;  and ___E:Varina Anne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varina_Anne_Davis)___ , born 1864, who remained single and lived to be 34.
In July 1845, Davis became a candidate for the ___E:United States House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ .

He ran on a platform emphasizing a ___E:strict constructionist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strict_constructionist)___ view of the constitution, ___E:states' rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States%27_rights)___ , tariff reductions, and opposition to a national bank. He won the election and entered the 29th Congress.
Davis opposed using federal monies for internal improvements, which he believed would undermine the autonomy of the states.
He supported the American annexation of Oregon, but through peaceful compromise with Britain.
On May 11, 1846, he voted for war with Mexico.

At the beginning of the ___E:Mexican–American War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War)___ , Mississippi raised a volunteer unit, the ___E:First Mississippi Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Mississippi_Regiment)___ , for the U.S.
Army.  Davis expressed his interest in joining the regiment if he was elected its colonel, and in the second round of elections in June 1846 he was chosen.
He did not give up his position as a U.S.
Representative, but left a letter of resignation with his brother Joseph to submit when he thought it was appropriate.

Davis was able to get his regiment armed with new ___E:percussion rifles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_cap#Military_firearms)___ instead of the ___E:smoothbore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoothbore)___ muskets used by other units. ___E:President Polk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Polk)___ approved their purchase as a political favor in return for Davis marshalling enough votes to pass the ___E:Walker Tariff U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_Tariff)___ .

Because of its association with the regiment, the weapon became known as the " ___E:Mississippi rifle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1841_Mississippi_Rifle)___ ",  and the regiment became known as the " ___E:Mississippi Rifles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/155th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States))___ ".
Davis's regiment was assigned to the army of his former father-in-law, Zachary Taylor, in northeastern Mexico.
Davis distinguished himself at the ___E:Battle of Monterrey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monterrey)___ in September by leading a charge that took the fort of La Teneria.
He then went on a two-month leave and returned to Mississippi, where he learned that Joseph had submitted Davis's resignation from the House of Representatives in October.

Davis returned to Mexico and fought in the ___E:Battle of Buena Vista U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Buena_Vista)___ on February 22, 1847. He was wounded in the heel during the fighting,  but his actions stopped an attack by the Mexican forces that threatened to collapse the American line.  In May, Polk offered him a federal commission as a ___E:brigadier general U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigadier_general_(United_States))___ .

Davis declined the appointment, arguing he could not directly command militia units because the ___E:U.S. Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Constitution)___ gives the power of appointing militia officers to the states, not the federal government.
Instead, he accepted an appointment by Mississippi governor ___E:Albert G. Brown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_G._Brown)___ to fill a vacancy in the U.S.
Senate  left when ___E:Jesse Speight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Speight)___ died.
Davis took his seat in December 1847 and was made a regent of the ___E:Smithsonian Institution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution)___ .

The ___E:Mississippi state legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_state_legislature)___ confirmed his appointment as ___E:senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senator)___ in January 1848.  He quickly established himself as an advocate of expanding slavery into the ___E:Western territories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_territories)___ .

He argued that because the territories were the common property of all the United States and lacked state sovereignty to ban slavery, slave owners had the equal right to settle them as any other citizens.

Davis tried to amend the ___E:Oregon Bill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Bill_of_1848)___ to allow settlers to bring their slaves into ___E:Oregon Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Territory)___ .

He opposed ratifying the ___E:Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Guadalupe_Hidalgo)___ , which ended the Mexican–American War, claiming that ___E:Nicholas Trist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Trist)___ , who negotiated the treaty, had done so as a private citizen and not a government representative.

Instead, he advocated negotiating a new treaty ceding additional land to the United States,  and opposed the application of the ___E:Wilmot Proviso U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmot_Proviso)___ to the treaty,  which would have banned slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico.
During the 1848 presidential election, Davis chose not to campaign against Zachary Taylor, who was the ___E:Whig candidate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States))___ .
After the Senate session following Taylor's inauguration ended in March 1849, Davis returned to ___E:Brierfield Plantation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brierfield_Plantation)___ .
He was reelected by the state legislature for another six-year term in the Senate.

Around this time, he was approached by the Venezuelan adventurer ___E:Narciso López U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narciso_L%C3%B3pez)___ to lead a ___E:filibuster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_(military))___ expedition to liberate Cuba from Spain.
He turned down the offer, saying it was inconsistent with his duty as a senator.
When Calhoun died in the spring of 1850, Davis became the senatorial spokesperson for the South.

The Congress debated ___E:Henry Clay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay)___ 's resolutions, which sought to address the sectional and territorial problems of the nation  and became the basis for the ___E:Compromise of 1850 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1850)___ .
Davis was against the resolutions because he felt they would put the South at a political disadvantage.
He opposed the admission of California as a free state without its first becoming a territory, asserting that a territorial government would give slaveowners the opportunity to colonize the region.
He also tried to extend the ___E:Missouri Compromise Line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Compromise_Line)___ to allow slavery to expand to the Pacific Ocean.

He stated that not allowing slavery into the new territories denied the political equality of Southerners,  and threatened to undermine the balance of power between Northern and Southern states in the Senate.

In the autumn of 1851, Davis was nominated to run for governor of Mississippi against ___E:Henry Stuart Foote U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Stuart_Foote)___ , who had favored the Compromise of 1850. He accepted the nomination and resigned from the Senate, but Foote won the election by a slim margin.

Davis turned down a reappointment to his Senate seat by outgoing Governor ___E:James Whitfield U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Whitfield_(Mississippi_politician))___ ,  settling in Brierfield for the next fifteen months.

He remained politically active, attending the Democratic convention in January 1852 and campaigning for Democratic candidates ___E:Franklin Pierce U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce)___ and ___E:William R. King U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_R._King)___ during the ___E:presidential election of 1852 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1852_United_States_presidential_election)___ .
In March 1853, President Franklin Pierce named Davis his ___E:Secretary of War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_War)___ .

He championed a ___E:transcontinental railroad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcontinental_railroad)___ to the Pacific Ocean, arguing it was needed for national defense,  and was entrusted with overseeing the ___E:Pacific Railroad Surveys U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Railroad_Surveys)___ to determine which of four possible routes was the best.  He promoted the ___E:Gadsden Purchase U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gadsden_Purchase)___ of today's southern ___E:Arizona U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona)___ from Mexico, partly because he preferred a southern route for the new railroad.

The Pierce administration agreed and the land was purchased in December 1853.  He presented the surveys' findings in 1855, but they failed to clarify the best route and sectional problems prevented any choice being made.  Davis also argued for the acquisition of Cuba from Spain, seeing it as an opportunity to add the island, a strategic military location and potential slave state.
He suggested that the size of the regular army was too small and that its salaries were too meagre.
Congress agreed and authorized four new regiments and increased its pay scale.

He ended the manufacture of smoothbore muskets and shifted production to rifles, working to develop the tactics that accompany them.  He oversaw the building of public works in Washington D.C., including the initial construction of the ___E:Washington Aqueduct U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Aqueduct)___ .

Davis assisted in the passage of the ___E:Kansas-Nebraska Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas-Nebraska_Act)___ in 1854 by allowing President Pierce to endorse it before it came up for a vote.  This bill, which created ___E:Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory)___ and ___E:Nebraska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska_Territory)___ territories, repealed the ___E:Missouri Compromise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Compromise)___ 's limits on slavery and left the decision about a territory's slaveholding status to ___E:popular sovereignty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_sovereignty#1850s)___ , which allowed the territory's residents to decide.
The passage of this bill led to the demise of the Whig party, which had tried to limit expansion of slavery in the territories.

It also contributed to the rise of the ___E:Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States)#19th_century)___ and the increase of ___E:civil violence in Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Kansas)___ .
The Democratic nomination for the 1856 presidential election went to ___E:James Buchanan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan)___ .

Knowing his term was over when the Pierce administration ended in 1857, Davis ran for the Senate once more and re-entered it on March 4, 1857.  In the same month, the ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court)___ decided the ___E:Dred Scott case U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sanford)___ , which ruled that slavery could not be barred from any territory.

The Senate recessed in March and did not reconvene until November 1857.  The session opened with a debate on the ___E:Lecompton Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecompton_Constitution)___ submitted by a convention in Kansas Territory.
If approved, it would have allowed Kansas to be admitted as a slave state.

Davis supported it, but it was not accepted, in part because the leading Democrat in the North, ___E:Stephen Douglas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Douglas)___ , argued it did not represent the true will of the settlers in the territory.
The controversy undermined the alliance between Northern and Southern Democrats.

Davis's participation in the Senate was interrupted in early 1858 by a recurring case of ___E:iritis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uveitis)___ , which threatened the loss of his left eye.  It left him bedridden for seven weeks.

During his years as a senator, Davis was an advocate for the Southern states' right to slavery.
In an 1848 speech on the Oregon Bill,  he argued for a ___E:strict constructionist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strict_constructionism)___ understanding of the Constitution.

He insisted that the states are sovereign, all powers of the federal government are granted by those states,  the Constitution recognized the right of states to allow citizens to have slaves as property, and the federal government was obligated to defend encroachments upon this right.
In his February 13–14, 1850 speech,  Davis declared that slaveholders must be allowed to bring their slaves into federal territories.
He stated that slavery does not need to be justified: it was sanctioned by religion and history.
He argued that African Americans were destined for bondage,  and their enslavement was a civilizing blessing to them  that brought economic and social good to everyone.
Davis's speeches after secession acknowledged the relationship between the Confederacy and slavery.

In his resignation speech to the Senate, delivered 12 days after his state seceded, he said Mississippi "has heard proclaimed the theory that all men are created free and equal, and this made the basis of an attack upon her social institutions and the sacred Declaration of Independence has been invoked to maintain the position of the equality of the races."  In his February 1861 inaugural speech as provisional president of the Confederacy,  Davis asserted that the Confederate Constitution, which explicitly prevented Congress from passing any law affecting African-American slavery and mandated its protection in all Confederate territories, was a return to the intent of the ___E:original founders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States)___ .

When he spoke to Congress in April on the ratification of the Constitution,  he stated that the war was caused by Northerners whose desire to end slavery would destroy Southern property worth millions of dollars."  In his 1863 address to the Confederate Congress,  Davis denounced the Emancipation Proclamation as evidence of the North's long-standing intention to abolish slavery and doom African Americans, whom he called an inferior ___E:race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(human_categorization))___ , to extermination.
Davis came to the role of commander in chief confident in his military abilities.
He had graduated from the United States Military Academy, served in the regular army, and commanded troops in combat.
He actively oversaw the military policy of the Confederacy and worked long hours attending to paperwork related to the organization, finance, and logistics needed to maintain the Confederate armies.
Some historians argue that Davis's personality contributed to the defeat of the Confederacy.
His constant attention to minor military details has been used to illustrate an inability to delegate,  which led him to lose focus on larger issues.

He has been accused of being a poor judge of generals:  appointing people—such as Bragg, Pemberton, and Hood—–who failed to meet expectations,  overly trusting long-time friends,  and retaining generals—like Joseph Johnston—long after they should have been removed.
His need to be seen as always in the right has also been described as a problem.
Historians have argued that the time spent vindicating himself took time away from pressing problems and accomplished little.

His reactions to criticism made unnecessary enemies  and created hostile relationships with the politicians and generals he depended on.  It has been argued that his focus on military victory at all costs undermined the values the South was fighting for, such as states' rights  and slavery,  but provided no alternatives to replace them.
Other historians have pointed out his strengths.
Davis quickly mobilized the Confederacy despite the South's focus on states' rights, and he stayed focused on gaining independence.
He was a skilled orator who attempted to share the vision of national unity.
He shared his message through newspapers, public speeches, and trips where he would meet with the public.

His policies sustained the Confederate armies through numerous campaigns, buoying Southern hopes for victory and undermining the North's will to continue the war.  A few historians have argued that Davis may have been one of the best people available to serve as commander in chief.

Though he was unable to win the war,  he rose to the challenge of the presidency,  pursuing a strategy that not only enabled the Confederacy to hold out as long as it did, but almost achieved its independence.

Although Davis served the United States as a soldier and a war hero, a politician who sat in both houses of Congress, and a cabinet officer,  his legacy is mainly defined by his role as president of the Confederacy.

After the Civil War, journalist ___E:Edward A. Pollard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_A._Pollard)___ , who first popularized the ___E:Lost Cause U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause)___ mythology,  placed much of the blame for losing the war on Davis.
Into the twentieth century, many biographers and historians have also emphasized Davis's responsibility for the Confederacy's failure to achieve independence.
Since the second half of the twentieth century, this assumption has been questioned.

Some scholars argued that he was a capable leader, while acknowledging his skills were insufficient to overcome the challenges the Confederacy faced  and exploring how his limitations may have contributed to the war's outcome.
Davis's standing among white Southerners was at a low point at the end of the Civil War,  but it rebounded after his release from prison.
After Reconstruction, he became a venerated figure of the white South,  and he was often depicted as a ___E:martyr U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyr)___ who suffered for his nation.
His birthday was made a legal holiday in six Southern states.
His popularity among white Southerners remained strong in the early twentieth century.

Around 200,000 people attended the unveiling of the ___E:Jefferson Davis Memorial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Davis_Memorial_(Richmond,_Virginia))___ at Richmond, Virginia, in 1907.  Mississippi officials honored him with ___E:a life-size likeness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Jefferson_Davis_(U.S._Capitol))___ in the ___E:National Statuary Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Statuary_Hall)___ at the ___E:U.S. Capitol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol)___ in 1931.  In 1961, a centennial celebration reenacted Davis's inauguration in Montgomery, Alabama, with fireworks and a cast of thousands in period costumes.
In the early twenty-first century, there were at least 144 Confederate memorials commemorating him throughout the United States.

On October 17, 1978, Davis's U.S. citizenship was posthumously restored after the Senate passed ___E:Joint Resolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_resolution)___ 16. President ___E:Jimmy Carter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter)___ described it as an act of reconciliation reuniting the people of the United States and expressing the need to establish the nation's founding principles for all.   However, Davis's legacy continued to spark controversy.
In the twenty-first century, most historians agree that Davis's participation in the Confederacy constituted treason.

His memorials, such as the ___E:Jefferson Davis Highway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Davis_Highway)___ , have been argued to legitimize the ___E:white supremacist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacist)___ , slaveholding ideology of the Confederacy,  and a number have been removed, including his statues at the ___E:University of Texas at Austin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin)___ ,  New Orleans,  Memphis, Tennessee,  and the ___E:Kentucky State Capitol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_State_Capitol)___ in Frankfort.
